title: arXiv AI weekly: 21 October 2026 batch — 6 notable papers
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; ordering is inferred from checkable attention/discussion and relevance signals. Citation evidence for these new papers is limited, and the available candidate pool is incomplete.

sections.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research
sections.abstract: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022–2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors contribute a bounded, end-to-end quantitative-research protocol connecting feature construction and iterative testing to a frozen strategy's sealed-period portfolio outcome.
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence covers one selected A-share universe and a single simulated out-of-sample year; it is not evidence of live-trading performance.

sections.title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
sections.abstract: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors provide a leaderboard for measuring robustness to unseen batches and sources using JUMP-CP, a Cell Painting dataset with pronounced distribution shifts.
sections.unique_caveat: The benchmark is grounded in one assay and dataset; its ranking does not by itself establish robustness across other biomedical modalities or acquisition pipelines.

sections.title: Agentic World Action Models
sections.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine code-based skill planning with predictive video and action generation in a coupled generative architecture, using automatically curated program-aligned demonstrations.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report that default AW-0 remains sensitive to visual randomization (20.6% success versus 80.8% in the clean setting); the real-world hybrid evaluation is limited to the tested platforms and tasks.

sections.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
sections.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose LongZero, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose a zero-external-data RL pipeline that separates compact task/evidence construction from expansion into long multi-document contexts.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported study covers two LLMs and five benchmarks; broader model families and deployment settings remain untested in the evidence summarized here.

sections.title: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
sections.abstract: Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model's underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors frame capability diagnosis as behavior-supervised tree induction and report that the resulting leaves reveal model differences obscured by aggregate benchmark scores.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors state that experiments use static, single-turn English benchmarks with deterministic scoring, and do not validate multi-turn, agentic, or open-ended settings; the method also incurs repeated LLM calls.

sections.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
sections.abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce test-time in-context calibration through a compact descriptor, without physics labels, fine-tuning, or analytical physics models.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors note that data must be grouped by physics configuration, calibration depends on the interaction prompt, and the approach assumes stationary physics within an episode.
